title: The Ga State: From the Hill to the Sea

pages.text: For about a month each year, usually in May and June, a hush falls over the old quarters of Accra. Drumming and loud music are forbidden. Then, in August, the silence breaks. Families cook kpokpoi, a dish of steamed maize served with palm-nut soup and fish. Chiefs walk through the streets sprinkling it on the ground for the ancestors, and people cheer. This is Homowo. The word means hooting at hunger. It is the great festival of the Ga people, who founded Accra, and behind it lies the story of a long journey and a hard beginning.

pages.text: Ga tradition says that their ancestors came from the east, some by land and some by canoe along the coast. By the 1500s, they had built a kingdom with its capital at Ayawaso, on a hill a few kilometres inland from the sea. Visitors called it Great Accra. In the earliest days, the Ga were led by priests called wulomei, who still play an important part in Ga life. Later, a king, the Ga Mantse, led the people in war and government. The hill gave a clear view of the plains and of anyone coming near.

pages.alt: A town on a low hill with a view across open plains to the distant sea.

pages.text: The Ga chose their place wisely. Gold came down from the forest states, and ships waited at the coast. Ayawaso stood between them. The Ga kings would not let inland traders go to the ships directly, and so all the trade had to pass through Ga hands. European companies asked the Ga for land on the shore. The Dutch built a fort in 1649, the Danes began Christiansborg in 1661, and the English built James Fort in 1673. For a time, the Ga state was one of the richest on the coast.

The Dutch built a fort in 1649, the Danes began Christiansborg in 1661, and the English built James Fort in 1673.

pages.alt: Three small forts standing along a shoreline with canoes drawn up on the beach.

pages.text: Wealth attracted a strong neighbour. Akwamu, in the hills to the north, wanted the coast trade for itself. In 1677, its army attacked Ayawaso. The Ga king, Okaikoi, was killed, and the capital was destroyed. Over the next few years, the Ga left the hill and moved down to the shore, settling beside the forts. There, six towns grew up side by side: Ga Mashie, Osu, La, Teshie, Nungua, and Tema. Each had its own chief and its own priests. Together they formed the Ga state as it is known today.

pages.alt: Families walking down from a hill towards the coast, carrying their belongings.

pages.text: By the sea, the Ga became expert fishermen and traders. Their long canoes, carved from single tree trunks and painted with sayings, still line the beaches at Jamestown and Teshie. The towns welcomed strangers. Freed people who returned from Brazil in the 1800s settled among the Ga and are remembered as the Tabom. In 1877, the British moved the capital of their Gold Coast colony from Cape Coast to Accra. The Ga towns slowly grew together into one city. In 1957, Accra became the capital of independent Ghana. The six towns had become the heart of a nation.

pages.text: And the hunger? Tradition says that when the Ga first settled, the rains failed and a terrible famine followed. The people did not give up. They planted again and waited. When at last the rain came, the harvest was so large that they feasted and jeered at the hunger that had tried to destroy them. Every Homowo repeats that moment. The quiet weeks before it allow the young crops to grow in peace. So the festival carries a message for everyone who lives in Accra today, whatever their language: do not give up in hard times, and remember who made this place a home.
